items.md: The paper estimates the causal effect of research university activity on wages paid by local firms outside higher education (p. 1–2). University activity is endogenous: productive local firms may attract university partnerships and demand its graduates, and spillovers can run in both directions (p. 2). The authors build an instrument from the fact that universities spend a roughly fixed share of endowment market value, interacting national stock market changes with each county's lagged endowment per capita (p. 4–5). The contribution is an identification strategy for university spillovers in the agglomeration literature, plus evidence that effects are persistent and larger where universities are more research intensive or local industries are technologically closer to them (p. 2–3). The headline is that a 10% increase in higher education spending raises noneducation labor income by 0.8% (p. 2).

**Design.** Long differences over three and five years for county $i$, industry $j$:
$$\Delta Y_{ijt} = \alpha_1 \Delta UE_{it} + T + \varepsilon_{ijt}$$
$$\Delta UE_{it} = \beta_1 (\Delta SM_t \times IE_{i,t-x-1}) + T + \nu_{it}$$
$\Delta Y$ is the long difference in log average noneducation labor income, $\Delta UE$ the long difference in per capita total university expenditure, $\Delta SM$ the change in the S&P 500, $IE$ lagged per capita endowment market value, and $T$ year effects (p. 4).

items.md: **Identifying assumption.** Without stock price changes, labor income in counties with different initial endowments would have grown at similar rates (p. 5). Time-invariant differences are differenced out.

q.exact: As stock market shocks and the level of the initial endowment are exogenous to trends in local economic activity across counties, this variation pro- vides a compelling source to identify the effects of overall university expenditures on local economies.

items.md: **Estimation.** Two-stage least squares, weighted by 1981 industry-county employment so estimates reflect the average worker (p. 6). Expenditure covers all revenue sources.

q.exact: Our goal in weighting the regression to account for employment in the industry-county-year cell is to capture the effect of university activity on the average worker within the county, as opposed to the average effect across all industries.

items.md: **Inference.** Standard errors clustered by county (p. 6); county-year clustering in robustness (Table 10).

items.md: **Wage spillovers.** OLS gives 0.064 (0.029) at three years and 0.071 (0.032) at five; TSLS gives 0.114 (0.036) and 0.115 (0.038) (Table 4, p. 10). The authors translate a one standard deviation ($1.01 per thousand residents) rise into 11.5% higher noneducation labor income, an elasticity of 0.08, $0.89 of added labor income per $1 of spending and a multiplier of about 1.9 (p. 10).

q.exact: Put another way, a $1 increase in university spending generates an 89 cent increase in noneducation labor income. We also find that these effects are persistent, at least measured out five years, thus suggesting that an expenditure shock to a university produces something more profound than a simple fiscal multiplier effect.

items.md: The instrument is clever and the long-difference design removes fixed county and industry differences, but it carries several threats. The shock is one national series, the S&P 500, and its main effect is absorbed by year effects, so identification comes entirely from cross-county differences in initial endowment per capita. Endowment-rich counties are older, higher-ranked, more private and more college-educated (Table 2, p. 9), so the exclusion restriction requires that no such characteristic leads to differential income trends when stocks rise. Table 11 allows quality, state, industry, rent and 1900 characteristics to interact with the shock and results hold, with the industry-trend estimate at 78% of baseline (p. 15–16). Even so, the stock boom in the sample (no negative three- or five-year returns, p. 5) can raise local wealth, donor giving and firm finance directly, and the paper's donations test is insignificant (Table 8) rather than decisive.

Instrument strength is borderline: F is near 13, falls to 8.01 in Table 7's five-year model, and to 6.16 and 7.55 in the unweighted results (Table 10). The unweighted estimates are about a quarter to a third of the baseline, so the headline applies to employment-weighted industries that are overrepresented in university counties.

TSLS exceeds OLS (0.114 against 0.064). The authors attribute this to measurement error, supported by trimming, but the estimate is also a local effect for endowment-driven expenditure changes at endowment-rich institutions.

The outcome is labor income, not productivity. Employment effects are not significant, composition and skill changes are not examined in this version, and spatial-equilibrium logic gives wages as both a lower bound (land rents) and an upper bound (migration frictions) on productivity gains (p. 3, 10). Total expenditure includes tuition and state support, and the endowment shock moves graduate enrollment (Table 8), so "knowledge spillovers" are inferred from splits, not isolated.

Relevance to the project: the instrument fails for two-year colleges, which have no meaningful endowments, and the sample is research universities in large counties with wage outcomes, not firm entry or patents. What does transfer is the county-by-industry panel from County Business Patterns and the proximity splits (labor pooling, patent citation, college-graduate intensity), which suggest testing whether college openings shift industry mix toward industries that hire the college's graduates.
The mechanism is untested; the authors call for analysis of how industries close to higher education respond (p. 17).
Effects are estimated only for large urban research-university counties, 1981–1996, before alternative endowment assets grew (p. 5–6).
Employment, firm entry and patent outcomes are not estimated; employment effects are imprecise (Table 5).
Heterogeneity splits are descriptive and not separately instrumented (Table 9).
Composition of the workforce behind average labor income is not addressed in this version.

The paper's policy message is that place-based university policy can raise local wages when focused on industries close to university knowledge (p. 17). For the project on two-year college openings, the exogenous-shock instrument is unavailable, so identification must come from openings or siting rules, not endowments. The design lessons are to use county-by-industry cells, weight by baseline employment, report weighted and unweighted estimates, and test heterogeneity by industry proximity to college outputs, such as labor pooling or share of college graduates. The persistence evidence (Tables 6 and 7) suggests allowing multi-year dynamic responses. Outcomes should extend to firms, industry mix and patents, which this paper does not examine.
